TMFG and LoGo information-filtering networks with the psychnets R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/information-filtering-networks.Rmd
information-filtering-networks.Rmd

A questionnaire with many items can yield so many correlations that the most informative relationships are difficult to see. Researchers studying motivation, self-efficacy and self-regulation may want to examine these constructs together, yet plotting every association creates a crowded network of variables connected by edges. Selecting edges solely through a significance threshold can likewise produce a dense graph that is difficult to interpret. Information-filtering networks offer a structured means of retaining a manageable set of associations while preserving a view of their interdependence. Filtering methods have been studied in psychometric network research (Christensen et al., 2018). Exploratory graph analysis also uses network structure, but for the distinct purpose of investigating dimensionality (Golino & Epskamp, 2017; Golino et al., 2020).

Information-filtering networks extract a sparse, connected backbone from an association matrix according to structural constraints rather than a significance test or a regularisation penalty. The Triangulated Maximally Filtered Graph (TMFG; Massara et al., 2016) constructs a planar graph from strong correlations and retains exactly 3(p−2)3(p - 2) edges for pp variables. The Local-Global method (LoGo; Barfuss et al., 2016) uses the cliques and separators of this graph to estimate a sparse precision matrix and its partial correlations, without selecting a penalty parameter. These methods therefore provide two related descriptions of the data: TMFG edges express ordinary pairwise correlations, whereas LoGo edges express conditional associations within the fitted model after accounting for the other variables. Neither kind of edge establishes a causal relationship.

Psychological networks have been used in educational research to investigate relationships among learning processes and their development over time. For example, Saqr et al. (2021) examined relational and temporal patterns of self-regulation in academic writing, and Malmberg et al. (2022) used network analysis to study associations between students’ monitoring events and phases of regulation. Saqr et al. (2024) discuss psychological network methods for analysing learning and complex learning processes more broadly. These applications illustrate why the pattern of connections among learning-related variables can be of substantive interest. They also make it important to distinguish a readable representation of associations from evidence about causal mechanisms, stable network structure or individual learners.

This article demonstrates TMFG and LoGo using five self-regulated learning construct scores supplied with the psychnets package. It first constructs a correlation-based TMFG backbone and checks its structural properties, then estimates LoGo partial correlations and examines their optimality, node centralities and predictability. Finally, it visualises the network, repeats the analysis using Spearman correlations and outlines reporting and interpretation considerations. The responses were generated by a language model rather than collected from students, so the example illustrates the methods and their interpretation rather than empirical conclusions about learners.

library(psychnets)

The model

TMFG begins with a set of four variables selected for their strong combined correlations, forming a tetrahedron with six edges. Each remaining variable is placed in the triangular face for which its connections to the three vertices have the greatest combined weight. The new variable is connected to those vertices, adding three edges. The construction therefore has

6+3(p−4)=3(p−2) 6 + 3(p - 4) = 3(p - 2)

edges, and the graph is connected, planar and chordal: it decomposes into four-node cliques that overlap in three-node separators.

LoGo uses this decomposition to estimate the precision matrix. With 𝐒\mathbf{S} the correlation matrix, 𝒞\mathcal{C} the four-node cliques and 𝒯\mathcal{T} the three-node separators,

𝐊̂=∑c∈𝒞[𝐒cc−1]0−∑t∈𝒯[𝐒tt−1]0, \widehat{\mathbf{K}} = \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} \left[\mathbf{S}_{cc}^{-1}\right]^{0} - \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \left[\mathbf{S}_{tt}^{-1}\right]^{0},

where [⋅]0[\cdot]^0 places a small inverse into the full p×pp \times p matrix with zeros elsewhere. The result is the maximum-likelihood precision matrix of a Gaussian model whose missing edges are exactly those absent from the TMFG, and the partial correlations are ρij⋅rest=−Kij/KiiKjj\rho_{ij \cdot \mathrm{rest}} = -K_{ij}/\sqrt{K_{ii}K_{jj}}.

Data

SRL_GPT contains 300 sets of responses to items from the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire, summarised as construct scores on a scale from 1 to 7. The responses were generated by a large language model (GPT) in a study of how such models answer psychological surveys (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). They provide a convenient worked example, but should not be interpreted as observations of students or their learning.

  • Nodes: five construct scores, treated as continuous: CSU (cognitive strategy use), IV (intrinsic value), SE (self-efficacy), SR (self-regulation) and TA (test anxiety).
  • Observations: one row per respondent; the data are complete.
head(SRL_GPT)
#>        CSU       IV       SE       SR   TA
#> 1 5.307692 5.666667 5.777778 5.333333 4.00
#> 2 5.846154 6.444444 6.000000 5.777778 4.00
#> 3 6.615385 6.666667 6.222222 6.333333 3.25
#> 4 5.692308 6.555556 6.333333 5.555556 4.50
#> 5 4.384615 5.555556 4.888889 4.777778 4.00
#> 6 4.846154 5.444444 5.666667 5.111111 3.50

With five nodes, a TMFG keeps 3(5−2)=93(5 - 2) = 9 of the 10 possible pairs, so the example shows how the method works rather than how much it filters. Filtering grows with the number of variables: with 30 items a TMFG keeps 84 of 435 pairs.

Which correlations form the backbone?

psychnet() with method = "tmfg" builds the filtered graph from the Pearson correlation matrix.

tmfg_net <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "tmfg")
summary(tmfg_net)
#> <psychnet> tmfg network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 9   (undirected)
#>   structural certificate (violated TMFG invariants): 0
#>   edge weight: range [-0.302, 0.861], mean 0.486
as.data.frame(tmfg_net)
#>   from to     weight
#> 1  CSU IV  0.8609975
#> 2  CSU SE  0.8345850
#> 3   IV SE  0.7846003
#> 4  CSU SR  0.8474352
#> 5   IV SR  0.8216346
#> 6   SE SR  0.7791388
#> 7  CSU TA -0.1385109
#> 8   IV TA -0.1137214
#> 9   SR TA -0.3019634

The backbone has 9 edges, with correlations from -0.302 to 0.861. The four learning constructs are fully connected by strong positive correlations, from 0.779 (SE–SR) to 0.861 (CSU–IV). Test anxiety is attached through three negative correlations, the strongest with self-regulation (-0.302). The excluded pair is SE–TA. TMFG chooses edges as part of a connected structure rather than by a cut-off, so an excluded pair is not necessarily uncorrelated.

Does the backbone have the required structure?

A TMFG is defined by its structure: exactly 3(p−2)3(p - 2) edges, connected, planar and chordal. certificate() counts how many of these properties the fitted graph violates.

certificate(tmfg_net)
#>   method certificate       kind certified
#> 1   tmfg           0 structural      TRUE

The count is 0 and certified is TRUE: the graph has all the properties of a TMFG. This checks the construction, not the stability of the selected edges across samples.

Which associations remain after adjustment?

psychnet() with method = "logo" builds the same backbone and estimates partial correlations on it.

logo_net <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "logo")
summary(logo_net)
#> <psychnet> logo network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 9   (undirected)
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 6.66e-16
#>   edge weight: range [-0.372, 0.404], mean 0.191
as.data.frame(logo_net)
#>   from to     weight
#> 1  CSU IV  0.4035714
#> 2  CSU SE  0.3934966
#> 3   IV SE  0.1648976
#> 4  CSU SR  0.3771675
#> 5   IV SR  0.3300708
#> 6   SE SR  0.1681288
#> 7  CSU TA  0.1100782
#> 8   IV TA  0.1463203
#> 9   SR TA -0.3720398

The LoGo network has the same 9 edges, now carrying partial correlations. The strongest positive edges join cognitive strategy use with intrinsic value (0.404), self-efficacy (0.393) and self-regulation (0.377). Self-regulation and test anxiety share the only negative edge (-0.372), slightly stronger than their correlation of -0.302.

Comparing the two tables shows what adjustment does. The IV–SE correlation is 0.785 but its partial correlation is 0.165. The association between intrinsic value and self-efficacy is therefore considerably smaller after adjustment for the other constructs. Test anxiety correlates negatively with cognitive strategy use (-0.139) and intrinsic value (-0.114), whereas its partial correlations with these constructs are positive (0.110 and 0.146). These changes of sign reflect conditional associations in the fitted network; they do not establish that self-regulation mediates the relationships. TMFG and LoGo weights should therefore be reported and interpreted separately.

Is the LoGo network the maximum-likelihood solution?

LoGo is a closed-form construction, and its result should be the maximum-likelihood estimate for the TMFG graph. Any such solution must satisfy the problem’s optimality (Karush–Kuhn–Tucker) conditions: the implied covariance reproduces the observed correlation on every retained edge and on the diagonal, and the precision is zero on every missing edge. The amount by which a fitted network violates them is its certificate; a value near zero shows that the network is the optimum of its objective.

certificate(logo_net)
#>   method  certificate kind certified
#> 1   logo 6.661338e-16  kkt      TRUE

The violation is at the level of machine precision (below 10−1410^{-14}), so the LoGo partial correlations are the maximum-likelihood estimates for the backbone.

Which constructs are most connected?

net_centralities() returns strength, the sum of absolute edge weights, and expected influence, the signed sum, for the LoGo network.

net_centralities(logo_net)
#>   node  strength expected_influence
#> 1  CSU 1.2843138          1.2843138
#> 2   IV 1.0448601          1.0448601
#> 3   SE 0.7265229          0.7265229
#> 4   SR 1.2474068          0.5033273
#> 5   TA 0.6284383         -0.1156412

Cognitive strategy use has the largest strength (1.284), equal to its expected influence because all its edges are positive. Self-regulation follows in strength (1.247), but its negative edge with test anxiety lowers its expected influence to 0.503. Test anxiety has the smallest strength (0.628) and a negative expected influence (-0.116). Cognitive strategy use is the most connected construct, and self-regulation is the link between the learning constructs and test anxiety. Centrality describes the graph and does not identify causes or intervention targets.

How well is each construct predicted by the others?

net_predict() reports each node’s R2R^2, computed from the LoGo precision matrix as Rj2=1−1/(KjjSjj)R_j^2 = 1 - 1/(K_{jj}S_{jj}).

net_predict(logo_net)
#>   node     type metric predictability accuracy
#> 1  CSU gaussian     R2      0.8347645       NA
#> 2   IV gaussian     R2      0.7824561       NA
#> 3   SE gaussian     R2      0.7227872       NA
#> 4   SR gaussian     R2      0.7923888       NA
#> 5   TA gaussian     R2      0.1589941       NA

In the fitted Gaussian network, the other constructs account for approximately 83% of the variance in cognitive strategy use (R2=0.835R^2 = 0.835), 79% in self-regulation, 78% in intrinsic value and 72% in self-efficacy, but only 16% in test anxiety (R2=0.159R^2 = 0.159). The learning constructs are largely predictable from one another, while test anxiety is not. These are in-sample values.

What does the network look like?

cograph::splot() draws the LoGo network, with green positive and red negative edges and a ring showing each node’s predictability.

cograph::splot(logo_net, psych_styling = TRUE, predictability = TRUE)

The figure shows the triangulated structure: four learning constructs fully connected, and test anxiety attached to three of them. Node positions come from a layout algorithm and carry no statistical meaning.

Do the conclusions depend on the correlation estimator?

Refitting LoGo with cor_method = "spearman" bases both the backbone and the partial correlations on rank correlations.

logo_spearman <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "logo",
                          cor_method = "spearman")
summary(logo_spearman)
#> <psychnet> logo network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 9   (undirected)
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 1.67e-15
#>   edge weight: range [-0.301, 0.440], mean 0.191
as.data.frame(logo_spearman)
#>   from to      weight
#> 1  CSU IV  0.41199792
#> 2  CSU SE  0.44035144
#> 3   IV SE  0.11746132
#> 4  CSU SR  0.34053654
#> 5   IV SR  0.36023514
#> 6   SE SR  0.15431277
#> 7  CSU TA  0.07122993
#> 8   IV TA  0.12358306
#> 9   SR TA -0.30091058
certificate(logo_spearman)
#>   method  certificate kind certified
#> 1   logo 1.665335e-15  kkt      TRUE

The rank-based backbone contains the same nine pairs. The positive edges of cognitive strategy use remain the strongest, with CSU–SE (0.440) now slightly above CSU–IV (0.412), and the SR–TA edge remains negative (-0.301). The weak CSU–TA edge falls from 0.110 to 0.071. The certificate is again at machine precision. For these data, the selected backbone and the principal associations are similar under the two correlation estimators.

Reporting the analysis

A report states the variables, the sample size, the correlation estimator and the treatment of missing data, and keeps the two stages apart: TMFG edges are correlations, LoGo edges are partial correlations.

In this analysis, TMFG on Pearson correlations of 300 complete responses kept 9 of 10 pairs, leaving out SE–TA. LoGo partial correlations on that backbone were largest for cognitive strategy use with intrinsic value (0.404) and negative only for self-regulation with test anxiety (-0.372). A rank-based analysis kept the same backbone and the same main edges.

Assumptions and when to use information filtering

  • TMFG fixes the number of edges at 3(p−2)3(p - 2) whatever the sample size. It suits large item sets where a readable backbone is wanted and where a penalty-based method would keep too many or too few edges; it does not test whether an edge is different from zero.
  • LoGo assumes a Gaussian model restricted to the TMFG graph. It needs no tuning parameter, but every four-node block of the correlation matrix must be invertible, so duplicated or perfectly collinear variables must be removed first.
  • When the aim is to select conditional associations using a statistical selection criterion, graphical lasso or stepwise selection may be more appropriate. When the aim is to display a sparse set of marginal associations, the TMFG backbone can be examined on its own.
  • Neither network identifies causal direction.
